records.text: Bill Erpenbeck served 21 years after pleading guilty in April 2003 to defrauding banks of 34 million dollars by diverting home-closing proceeds, leaving hundreds of buyers liable for unpaid mortgages
records.speaker: Anonymous Source #1 (Ep cZxHqYsWRYg)

appearances.snippet: Bill Erpenbeck served 21 years after pleading guilty to defrauding banks of $34 million. That was back in April of 2003. ... So he was a home builder who funneled the proceeds from home closings back to his company and himself. ... So his crimes left hundreds of homebuyers on the hook for millions of dollars in unpaid mortgages.

verification.notes: The Sixth Circuit records a 33.9-million-dollar diversion of buyers' closing checks, 260 purchasers and 224 uncleared liens, and Bill Erpenbeck's fraud plea and sentence history. Current local reporting confirms his April 2003 plea and 2024 release after about 21 years.

sources.title: United States v. A. William Erpenbeck, Jr. (Sixth Circuit, 2008)
sources.relevance: Official appellate opinion documents the fraud method, 33.9-million-dollar diversion, victims, plea, and sentence history.

sources.title: Bill Erpenbeck released after serving 20 years for fraud
sources.relevance: Current reporting confirms the April 2003 plea and release after approximately 21 years.

records.text: Lori Ann Erpenbeck told her lawyer that Tony Erpenbeck offered money to change her testimony about Bill Erpenbeck, after which the FBI arranged for her to wear a wire
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: Pardon, Tony (Tony Erpenbeck) offered her money to change her testimony about Bill (Bill Erpenbeck). Lori (Lori Ann Erpenbeck) told her lawyer about the conversation and the FBI was looped in. ... She agreed to wear a wire to capture information.

verification.notes: The Sixth Circuit states that Lori contacted the FBI, wore a wire, and recorded Bill and Anthony Erpenbeck urging false testimony and offering financial help if she testified as requested. This directly supports the account in transcript context.

sources.title: United States v. A. William Erpenbeck, Jr. (Sixth Circuit, 2008)
sources.relevance: Official opinion states Lori wore an FBI wire and was offered financial help to give requested testimony.

records.text: A notary testified that Bill Erpenbeck sometimes asked her to notarize documents when the purported signers were not present
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: Another personal favorite portion of mine from the news of that day is the notary testifying that Rick (Richard Erpenbeck)'s brother Bill (Bill Erpenbeck) would sometimes ask her to notarize documents while the person involved was not even present, right? ... She said Bill Erpenbeck sometimes asked her to notarize documents from the people who supposedly had signed them or not in her presence.

verification.notes: Transcript context recounts alleged notary testimony in the Erpenbeck matter. The reviewed appellate opinions and current searches did not expose the underlying testimony or a reliable source containing this exact account.

sources.title: Bride Of Charlie: Have No Fear, Lori Is Here. | Episode 3
sources.relevance: Primary transcript provenance for the allegation; this source does not independently corroborate it, as documented in the verification note.

records.text: Bill Erpenbeck received a 30-year sentence and served 21 years after a later reduction, while Tony Erpenbeck received additional prison time for the murder-and-kidnap plot
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: The recording is played in court. They get him. They get Tony (Tony Erpenbeck). Bill (Bill Erpenbeck) pleads guilty. He picks up additional charges for threatening to kill his sister. ... He's ultimately sentenced to 30 years in prison. He ends up serving 21 years after a judge later shortens his sentence. ... He later received another 20 years because, you know, he tried to hire the hitman to kill the U.S. district judge, the U.S. attorney, and the FBI agent's children.

verification.notes: Court records and current reporting confirm Bill Erpenbeck initially received a 30-year term, was resentenced to 25 years, and served about 21 years. The reviewed sources did not conclusively establish the statement's separate assertion that Tony received additional prison time for the murder-and-kidnapping plot, so the combined statement is only partly verified.

sources.title: United States v. A. William Erpenbeck, Jr. (Sixth Circuit, 2008)
sources.relevance: Official opinion documents Bill Erpenbeck's original and reduced federal sentence history.

sources.title: Bill Erpenbeck released after serving 20 years for fraud
sources.relevance: Current report confirms he served about 21 years before release.

records.text: In 2009 FBI agents recovered a cooler of cash buried at Summit Hills Country Club that Bill Erpenbeck intended to use after prison
records.speaker: Anonymous Source #1 (Ep cZxHqYsWRYg)

appearances.snippet: The Erpenbeck name was back in the news in 2009 when FBI agents dug up a cooler full of cash from Summit Hills Country Club in Crestview Hills. ... A friend had buried money that he received from Erpenbeck on the course next to Erpenbeck's former home. ... Erpenbeck had hoped to use that money after he got out of prison.

verification.notes: The Sixth Circuit's 2012 opinion states that FBI agents found more than 250,000 dollars in a cooler buried at a private golf course and that it was being held for Bill Erpenbeck until his release. Current reporting identifies the Summit Hills site and 2009 recovery.

sources.title: United States v. A. William Erpenbeck, Jr. (Sixth Circuit, 2012)
sources.relevance: Official opinion documents the FBI recovery of more than 250,000 dollars buried in a cooler for Erpenbeck's later use.

records.text: Bill Erpenbeck served more than two decades in prison for financial fraud, tried to kill or threatened to kill his sister, and buried cash on a golf course.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: Rick Erpenbeck is his name, whose brother Bill (Bill Erpenbeck) did... Over two decades in prison for financial fraud, you know, trying to kill his sister, threatening to kill his sister, burying cash on a golf course, just run of the mill stuff, you know.

verification.notes: Court records support the roughly 20-year-plus federal sentence, large fraud, and buried golf-course cash. Reporting says he contemplated killing his sister and tried to induce false testimony, but does not establish the statement's stronger wording that he tried or threatened to kill her.

sources.title: United States v. Erpenbeck et al., No. 11-3530 (6th Cir. 2012)
sources.relevance: Documents the fraud, 300-month sentence, and money buried near a golf course.

sources.title: Murder schemes, buried money and betrayal | Cincinnati Enquirer
sources.relevance: Reports more than 20 years served and distinguishes thoughts about killing his sister from efforts to obtain false testimony.

records.text: William Erpenbeck Jr. transferred 50% of his B&G Holdings stock to Bill Erpenbeck Children LLC, which Richard William Erpenbeck managed.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: We continue the second reason is that Bill (William Erpenbeck Jr.) transferred 50% of the stock that he owned in B&G Holdings LLC, and that's Bill (William Erpenbeck Jr.), his brother, the one that goes to prison for years. Well, we learned that Bill (William Erpenbeck Jr.) transferred 50% of that stock to an LLC called Bill (William Erpenbeck Jr.) Erpenbeck Children LLC, and Rick (Richard William Erpenbeck) managed that LLC.

verification.notes: The Kentucky Supreme Court opinion states Bill Erpenbeck transferred his 50% interest in B&G Properties to Bill Children LLC and that Richard Erpenbeck was the LLC's managing member.

sources.title: Richard Erpenbeck v. Kentucky Bar Association
sources.relevance: Kentucky Supreme Court opinion confirms the B&G stock transfer and Richard's management role.
